answers.answer: They dropped speech recognition and kept the LCD screen. The stated reason for keeping the screen was that it carried the whole concept — B said losing it would mean "we lose our whole concept," and D added that the LCD is more useful than speech and that the remote needs at least one innovation. Speech went first because it had never actually been integrated into the system (A had earlier said speech commands could just be mapped onto existing functions with no extra design), and cutting it saved four Euros against the twelve-and-a-half Euro cost ceiling.

answers.answer: They first leaned toward a flexible/spongy rubber case ("stress ball" material), and in the final meeting switched to a plastic solid single-curve case, keeping only a rubber grip. The stated reason was budget: the design was four Euros over, mostly from the LCD plus advanced chip, and plastic "incurs no cost" while rubber cost two Euros per unit, so the case material and shape were the trade-off used to get back under price.

answers.answer: The find-the-lost-remote feature was proposed in meeting 1 (speaker D: "Always gets lost. Some sort of like device to help you find it"), adopted in meeting 2 after marketing data showed 50% of respondents called losing the remote their biggest frustration, then dropped in meeting 4 — "we've decided not to worry about that for now." The main objection came from the industrial designer (speaker C in ES2008d), who said it would be difficult technologically because a lost remote is probably under the settee where an infrared signal cannot reach it, and that it might be "more just a gimmick" than anything else. Supporting reasons were that a chip/circuit-board noise approach "would take a lot more development than we have this afternoon" (B) and that the bright designs make the remote easy to spot; the ledger also records that the costing tool had no such option.

answers.answer: The complaint was raised in meeting 2 by D, the marketing member, who described repetitive strain injury (RSI) — the risk that people who watch a lot of TV and keep changing channels hurt their wrists from repeated button pressing. The team responded by making the case and buttons squeezable rubber and marketing it as anti-RSI (A also asked for medical background research on RSI and for legal to be consulted about future injury claims), while rejecting an iPod-style scroll wheel as worse for RSI; D objected that rubber push-buttons still involve repetitive movement, and A countered that repetition, not button type, causes RSI. By the meeting 4 evaluation the remote was scored 'very good' (one) against RSI and the anti-RSI claim was kept as the marketable novelty.

answers.answer: Team IS1002 began with twenty-five Euros as the selling price, which speaker D in IS1002b clarified was actually a wholesale price rather than retail. By the third meeting they had moved upmarket and settled on a sales bracket of thirty-five to fifty Euros, driven by brand-over-profit reasoning and the added cradle, locator and scroll-wheel features. Speaker D in IS1002b pushed hardest for a higher, more exclusive price, arguing to sell it wholesale for fifty to sixty Euros as "the Rolls Royce of remote controls" after earlier floating eighty-nine Euros; speaker letters are local to each meeting, so this refers to the marketing-oriented participant in IS1002b.

answers.answer: They chose real elderly users, sixty to eighty ("Now you're talking about sixty to eighty"), rather than a broad forty-plus/international market, because elderly people tend to have a hard time with new devices, so a small screen explaining each button was judged a good fit and the segment was seen as good for the company image. In the final meeting this was widened again: since the scroll wheel leans younger, the chair opted to sell to everybody and reach younger buyers with changeable fancy front covers instead of a re-focus.

answers.answer: The touch screen was dropped in meeting 3 (ES2009c), where A closed the discussion with "we will omit the touch screen in favour of voice recognition" — voice recognition was the feature kept, pitched by D as the lower-risk option that could reach market sooner. The cost estimate that drove the decision came from B (the industrial designer): "upwards of seventeen fifty Euro per remote", offered explicitly as a rough estimate against the twelve fifty cost goal. Note the figure is spoken as "seventeen fifty"; the number parser read it as 17.5 EUR, but A's follow-up ("if you multiply seventeen fifty by two that's thirty five") indicates seventeen-and-a-half, i.e. roughly 17.50 Euro per unit.

answers.answer: They kept the headline innovations — voice recognition, the LCD, the spinning wheel integrated with the LCD, advanced chip, rubber case, simple battery. To get under the twelve-point-five-Euro cap they replaced the scroll wheel with two side pushbuttons for volume, dropped the sample sensor as the most expensive item, and swapped the sample speaker for a simple beeper; the locator went as a gimmick, though the beeper still gives the locate beep. That left them "way under budget," with only special-colour cost left uncertain and flagged to management.

The final design in meeting 4 dropped kinetic and used battery only, confirmed when B asked whether kinetic was still in and was told no, with cost restraints cited as the reason.

answers.answer: They kept one fruit/vegetable shape — the broccoli-shaped squishy handheld — and dropped the idea of distinct fruit shapes, moving the theme to colour and printed fruit patterns instead. The stated reasons were comfort and cost: the other fruit shapes were judged too big and awkward to hold (though the broccoli felt comfortable, "like sorta like a joystick"), and different colours or prints are cheaper than different moulded shapes, with irregular shapes also costing more to produce and risking annoyance for users used to one button shape. In meeting 3 the theme's placement was still unresolved ("where are the fruit and vegetables now?" — "We we don't know"), with a suggestion it lived in the colour of the plastic face or the squishy part; meeting 4 is where the shape decision was actually settled.
